name: Pine Assistant AI
tagline: An AI assistant that calls, emails, and argues with companies on your behalf to cancel subscriptions, dispute charges, and lower bills.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The chat interface is the cheap part. The actual product is an agent that dials a bank's support line, survives twelve minutes of IVR hell, says the right words to a retention rep, and does it again tomorrow when the first rep lied. That means telephony, voice models tuned for noisy phone audio, per-company IVR maps, recording consent rules that differ by state, and a growing archive of which scripts actually produce a credit. You can one-shot the part that drafts a good dispute letter and tracks your cases. You cannot one-shot the part that sits on hold.
coreLoopDIY: A local case tracker that drafts dispute letters, cancellation emails, and phone scripts per company, then nags you about response deadlines.
requirements: Your own email account for sending, or just copy-paste
Willingness to make the phone calls yourself
whatYouLose: Outbound calls: the agent waiting on hold and talking to a human so you do not have to
Per-company knowledge of phone trees, retention offers, and which department actually has authority
Escalation paths that work, regulatory complaint templates, and knowing when to invoke them
Call recording handled within consent law instead of you guessing
Persistence: automatic follow-up when the first rep does nothing
moatNotes: Every completed call teaches it which phrase got a credit from which company. That archive is the product and it compounds.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the painful part of cancelling a gym membership or disputing a $180 overdraft fee was never writing the letter, it was the forty minutes of hold music and the rep whose job is to wear you down. People pay to never do that again. A local tool that hands you a perfect script still hands you the phone, and most people will leave the tab open for three weeks and eat the charge.
notes: The letter drafter is a weekend build; the hold music is not. The moat is a telephony stack plus a growing record of which exact words make which company refund you.
prompt:
Build a local-only "dispute desk" web app. Stack: Next.js App Router with TypeScript, SQLite via better-sqlite3, Tailwind. No auth, no cloud, no telemetry. Single user on localhost.

Data model:
- Company: name, support phone, support email, known cancellation URL, notes.
- Case: company, type (cancel | dispute_charge | lower_bill | refund | complaint), amount, account number, opened date, status (drafting | sent | awaiting_reply | escalated | won | lost), desired outcome.
- Event: case id, date, channel (phone | email | chat | mail), who said what, outcome, next action, next action due date.
- Artifact: case id, kind (letter | email | phone_script | regulator_complaint), generated text, created date.

Features:
1. Case list with status filter and a "needs action today" view driven by next action due dates.
2. Case detail page: timeline of events, add-event form, artifacts list.
3. Generate artifacts with an LLM. Read OPENAI_API_KEY from .env.local. One server action per artifact kind, each with its own prompt template stored in /lib/templates as editable TS files. The phone script template must output a numbered opening statement, three likely rep objections with responses, an explicit ask, and an escalation line.
4. Letter and email artifacts render as copyable plain text and as a printable page. No sending. The user sends them.
5. Export a case to a single markdown file for small claims or a regulator form.

Explicitly out of scope: placing phone calls, speech to text, IVR navigation, call recording, OAuth into any bank or billing provider, scraping company sites. Do not pretend to do these.

Seed the database with ten common companies and leave the phone and email fields blank with a comment that the user fills them in.

Deliver: npm install, npm run dev, a .env.local.example, and a README that states plainly that this drafts and tracks, and the user still makes the call.
